blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are now used as zero-shot judges of image quality, but their color judgments are rarely tested with colorimetric ground truth. We present a five-task benchmark based on the CIE colorimetric framework: AWB pair judgment, skin-tone bias direction, CCT estimation, CIE Delta E 2000 pair ordering, and color naming under changing illuminants. We test eight MLLM endpoints, including four Qwen3-VL variants, GLM-4.5V, GPT-5.4, Claude-Opus-4.7, and Gemini-3.1-Pro. The models often solve coarse binary AWB judgments, but they remain weak on numeric CCT estimation and on some fine color-difference judgments. On ColorChecker-24 stimuli, the three closed-weight frontier models reach CCT MAE of 715-1056 K, compared with 1358-2133 K for the five open-weight models. A non-ColorChecker control shows that this advantage is partly template-dependent. The results suggest that current MLLMs have useful color words and coarse visual priors, but their color judgments are not reliably calibrated to CIE-computable color differences.
blocks.zh: 多式联运大语言模型(MLLMs)现在被作为图像质量的零镜头判断器使用,但其色彩判断很少被用色度地真能测试. 我们提出了一个基于CIE色度框架的五大任务基准: AWB配对判断,皮肤通向偏向方向,CCT估计,CIE Delta E 2000配对定购,以及变化光子下的颜色命名. 我们测试了8个MLLM端点,包括4个Quen3-VL变体,GLM-4.5V,GPT-5.4,克洛德-奥普斯-4.7和双子座-3.1-Pro. 这些模型往往能解决粗细的二进制AWB判断,但在数值CCT估计和一些精细的分色判断上仍然很弱. 在ColorChecker-24的刺激上,三种闭量边框型号达到了715-1056 K的CCT MAE,而五个开量边框型号的闭量边框型号为1358-2133 K. 非ColorChecker控制显示,这种优势部分依赖于模板. 结果表明,目前的MLLMs有有用的色彩单词和粗糙的视觉前缀,但其色彩判断不可靠地被校正为CIE-可计算色彩差异.

blocks.en: Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Color is a core concern of any imaging pipeline. Cameras, displays,
and printers all spend large compute budgets on white balance, color
correction, and tone mapping, and all of these are tuned against
physical color measurements. Multimodal large language models
(MLLMs) are now being used in this pipeline as zero-shot
quality judges [ 1 , 2 ] ,
but few benchmarks isolate color judgment against
colorimetrically computable ground truth.

blocks.en:
Color is one of the few visual attributes with a computable
ground truth. Unlike object recognition or counting, color has
standardized chromatic-adaptation transforms, correlated color
temperature (CCT) loci, CIELab, and Δ ​ E 2000 \Delta E_{2000} formulas,
which together let us quantify errors in colorimetric units
without human annotation. This is the property our benchmark uses.

blocks.en:
We build on two recent lines of work. The MLLM-IQA
work [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] shows that MLLMs can be prompted as visual judges,
but its stimuli mix many low-level cues (sharpness, noise, exposure)
and do not isolate color as a single variable. The generative-color
work [ 4 , 5 ] shows that even flagship T2I models miss
named colors, but it tests generation , not perception .
Our benchmark targets the perception side and uses the standard
ColorChecker-24 stimulus design from classical color-constancy
research [ 7 , 8 ] .

blocks.en:
Contributions In this paper, we (1) introduce a
five-task color benchmark whose ground truth is computed from the
CIE colorimetric framework [ 9 ] , not from human
annotation; (2) evaluate eight MLLM endpoints across four vendors
and show that coarse AWB judgments, numeric CCT estimation,
perceptual Δ ​ E 2000 \Delta E_{2000} ordering, and grounded color naming
fail in different ways; and (3) separate the observed failures
into endpoint-family effects (warm-bias and Δ ​ E \Delta E ordering
plateau within Qwen), a daylight-band CCT central-tendency prior
shared by the open-weight cluster, a D65-grounded naming
bottleneck on Task E, and a model-specific pick-vs-name asymmetry
in Claude-Opus-4.7. The benchmark, raw responses, and analysis
scripts are released.

blocks.en: Related work
blocks.zh: 相关工作

blocks.en:
Recent MLLM-as-judge benchmarks evaluate aesthetic, document, and
low-level image quality with human labels [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , but their
stimuli mix sharpness, exposure, noise, layout, and semantics, and
do not isolate color against computable ground truth. A parallel
line on generative color fidelity reports that text-to-image
models often miss named colors or over-saturate
them [ 4 , 5 ] , but it
tests generation rather than perception. Classical color-constancy
benchmarks such as Gehler–Shi and SFU
automatic white balance (AWB) [ 7 , 8 ] provide the
ColorChecker stimulus convention and illuminant-estimation context,
to which recent learning-based methods add pure-color and
cross-sensor priors [ 13 ] . We reuse that
stimulus convention to evaluate prompt-based MLLMs rather than
specialised AWB networks. Language-only color-cognition
work [ 6 ] motivates our interpretation of
vocabulary-driven naming failures.

blocks.en: Method
blocks.zh: 方法

blocks.en:
The benchmark contains five tasks that test different parts of
MLLM color judgment: pair-wise discrimination (Tasks A and D),
direction naming (Task B), numeric regression (Task C), and
cross-illuminant naming consistency (Task E). All stimuli are
generated with CIE colorimetric formulas. Tasks A–D have
colorimetric ground truth, and Task E uses a fixed
Lab-nearest-neighbor color-name reference. All prompts return
single-line JSON, so the benchmark can run on any
OpenAI-compatible endpoint without model-specific code.
Fig. 2 shows one representative stimulus per task.

实验室近邻彩名参考. 所有提示返回

Task A — AWB pair judgment The model sees two
ColorChecker24 charts in random order, differing only in white
balance: one adapted to D65, the other multiplied by a fixed
R/B/G/M cast gain in linear sRGB. The model picks the
correctly-balanced image and names the cast direction. 24 pairs:
4 cast types × \times 6 CCTs. Prompts are zero-shot with a fixed
JSON schema; the cast label refers to the incorrect image (full
prompts in the released repo).

Task E — color naming under illuminant The
same underlying ColorChecker patch value is rendered with no
chromatic adaptation under T ∈ { 2700 , 4200 , 6500 , 7500 , 9000 } T\in\{2700,4200,6500,7500,9000\} K. The model names the color from the 11 basic-color
terms of Berlin & Kay (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple,
pink, brown, black, gray, white). The D65 reference name is
assigned by Δ ​ E a ​ b \Delta E_{ab} nearest-neighbour to ISCC-NBS
centroids in CIELab; there is no human annotation in the
evaluation loop. 40 stimuli (8 patches × \times 5 illuminants).
The raw constancy index is the per-patch fraction of renderings
that get the same dominant name; FM4 reports the conditional
variant.

Stimulus generation All stimuli follow four
design rules. First, every correct answer can be computed from CIE
015:2018 colorimetric formulas [ 9 ] , so no annotator is
needed. Second, each stimulus varies along a single color dimension
while luminance, layout, and image content are held fixed. Third,
prompts are zero-shot with a single fixed template per task,
temperature = 0 =0 , and no in-context examples, so reported scores
reflect the model’s prior rather than prompt engineering. Fourth,
stimuli are 480 × \times 320 PNGs and prompts return single-line
JSON, so the benchmark runs against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint
with no changes.

blocks.en:
Models and protocol We evaluate eight MLLMs from
four vendors. The Qwen3-VL family gives the primary axis: four
variants on a single training stack isolate parameter scale and reasoning mode — Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (small dense),
30B-A3B-Instruct (Mixture-of-Experts, MoE; 3B active), 32B-Instruct (dense flagship),
and 32B-Thinking (chain-of-thought). GLM-4.5V (Zhipu, 106B) is a
cross-family probe trained on an independent corpus and visual
encoder. The April 2026 closed-weight frontier models — GPT-5.4
(OpenAI), Claude-Opus-4.7 (Anthropic), and
Gemini-3.1-Pro-preview (Google) — serve as a contrastive
control. A failure that survives the Qwen → \to GLM probe but
breaks here points to a shared-prior origin rather than a
single-stack artifact. Qwen and GLM are accessed via SiliconFlow; the three
frontier models via OpenRouter (model IDs openai/gpt-5.4 , anthropic/claude-opus-4.7 , google/gemini-3.1-pro-preview ). All calls use
temperature = 0 =0 and max_tokens = 512 =512 ; the larger cap
accommodates the Thinking variant’s chain-of-thought. Because
closed-weight endpoints can change without notice, all raw
responses (including the call timestamps) are released with the
benchmark.

blocks.en: Experiments and results
blocks.zh: 实验和结果

blocks.en:
We report headline accuracy on each of the five tasks
(Table 1 ), then examine five repeated failure patterns
(FM1–FM5) followed by a non-ColorChecker robustness check.
Statistical intervals throughout are 1000-resample bootstrap 95%
CIs unless noted otherwise.

blocks.en:
Failure mode 2: 5500 K central-tendency anchor
(shared-prior cluster) Five of eight models return CCT values in
a narrow daylight band regardless of the true
illuminant (Fig. 3 A). The most extreme case is
Qwen-32B-Instruct, which returns 5500 K for all 27 of 27 stimuli — a single-value predictor whose response is
independent of the input. The other four anchored models cluster
in the daylight band but with model-specific anchors (e.g. Qwen-30B-MoE collapses to 3500 K and 5000 K but never 5500 K;
Qwen-8B is bimodal at 5500/5000 K). The shared property is
therefore a daylight-band central-tendency regression, not a
literal 5500 K collapse. Note that 5500 K is closer to D55
( ∼ \sim 5503 K) than to D65 (6504 K) and lies below the K-space
midpoint ( ∼ \sim 6350 K) and median (5700 K) of our GT — more
consistent with an sRGB-encoding prior than a D65-illuminant
prior. Mean absolute error (Fig. 3 B, blue bars)
splits into two clusters: 1358–2133 K for the five anchored
models and 715–1056 K for the three frontier closed-weight
models, a 2 2 – 3 × 3\times reduction (per-model values in
Table 1 ).
Within-500 K rate (orange bars) tells the same story: Claude
reaches 0.556 ( ∼ 5 × \sim 5\times the Qwen-8B baseline), and the only
anchored model that gets within striking distance is
Qwen-32B-Thinking at 0.333.

blocks.en:
The cross-family test rules out a single-model-family effect:
GLM-4.5V, trained on an independent corpus and visual encoder,
also clusters its 27 predictions in the 5500–6500 K band. But
the three frontier closed-weight models break the anchor: GPT-5.4
tracks identity within ∼ \sim 700 K on average, Claude-Opus-4.7
reaches the highest within-500 K rate, and Gemini-3.1-Pro spreads
its predictions across the full 2700–10000 K range. The shared anchor across Qwen and GLM points to a common prior
inside the open-weight cluster, but our experiments do not
identify the source: candidate explanations include over-
representation of daylight-balanced sRGB photography in the
open-weight pretraining ecosystem and reinforcement learning from
human feedback (RLHF) preference tuning that shapes numeric
outputs in the closed-weight models. Neither is
testable from the benchmark alone.

Robustness check: non-ColorChecker control As
ColorChecker-24 is heavily seen in training data, we re-rendered
Task C with 24 random sRGB-cube patches (identical pipeline
otherwise) and re-ran all 8 models. GPT-5.4
(715 K → \to 1417 K), Gemini-3.1-Pro (1056 K → \to 1793 K),
and Qwen-32B-Thinking (1358 K → \to 2189 K, the largest
degradation in the panel) all lose substantial accuracy without
the CC template, indicating that the frontier and chain-of-thought advantages
come partly from template-recognition priors.
Qwen-32B-Instruct holds at 1922 K, confirming its daylight-band
anchor is a model property and not a template artifact.
Claude-Opus-4.7 is the only model that improves on
template removal (978 K → \to 752 K).

Discussion
blocks.zh: 讨论情况

blocks.en:
The eight-model set lets us group the findings by what changes
across models: model family, vendor access tier, or single-model
identity. We discuss practical use, failure grouping, and
limitations in turn.
blocks.zh:

身份证明 我们讨论实际用途,失败分组,和
反过来限制。

blocks.en:
Use in color-aware pipelines Today’s MLLMs
cannot replace classical camera-characterisation tools for fine
color judgments. That said, GPT-5.4 and Gemini-3.1-Pro both score 1.000 on both
halves of Task A. Flagship MLLMs can therefore serve as coarse screening checks in pipelines where no physical
ground truth is on hand. As order-of-magnitude calibration points: human chromatic
illumination-discrimination thresholds reported by Pearce et
al. [ 11 ] are on the order of ∼ \sim 3–7 perceptual u ′ ​ v ′ u^{\prime}v^{\prime} steps near a 6700 K daylight reference; we do not project
this onto Kelvin because Kelvin is not perceptually uniform. On
the engineering side, classical learning-based AWB on
Gehler–Shi reaches mean angular error ∼ 1.78 ∘ \sim\!1.78^{\circ} [ 12 ] , well below the
chromatic-discrimination range of any MLLM in our evaluation. The frontier MLLM CCT MAE of
715–1056 K therefore falls in a range comparable in magnitude to
reported human illumination-discrimination thresholds near
daylight, while remaining far from specialised AWB systems. The open-weight cluster sits well above this floor on
CCT but matches frontier on binary AWB, so the pipeline choice
depends on whether the downstream task asks for a binary judgment
or a numeric Kelvin reading.

A failure-mode taxonomy The matrix sorts FM1–FM5
into four classes that a single-family study cannot tell apart: Qwen-family-specific (FM1, FM3 — warm-bias and Δ ​ E \Delta E plateau, source unidentified by the benchmark); shared-prior cluster (FM2 — daylight-band anchor that
survives the Qwen → \to GLM probe but breaks at the
open-weight → \to frontier boundary); D65-grounded naming
bottleneck (FM4 — across all eight models, read as a possible
ceiling under this stimulus/prompt protocol, not architectural);
and model-specific (FM5 Claude pick-vs-name, kept as one
hypothesis among several).

blocks.en:
Limitations Stimuli are synthetic charts, not
natural scenes; a future version will use SFU AWB and Gehler–Shi
photographs. Three caveats: (a) pipeline confounds —
the metameric shortcut (sRGB values treated as reflectance under
D65) and the different visual-encoder tokenisation across the
eight models may both contribute to cross-model differences,
especially on Task A; v2 will use measured BabelColor spectra and
report tokenisation statistics. (b) prompt sensitivity —
a single fixed prompt per task cannot separate prompt effects
from chromatic perception; a 3-prompt ablation is deferred to v2.
(c) numeric output confound — CCT-in-Kelvin may test
calibrated numeric output as much as chromatic estimation; a
CCT-bin classification variant will accompany the regression in
v2. Without a human baseline we cannot claim MLLMs are worse than humans, only that they do not match
colorimetric ground truth; a 30-participant study on Tasks A and
B is underway.

blocks.en: Conclusion
blocks.zh: 结论

blocks.en:
We introduced a five-task, CIE-computable benchmark for
evaluating MLLM color judgment. Across eight endpoints, coarse AWB decisions
are often solved, but CCT estimation, Δ ​ E 2000 \Delta E_{2000} ordering,
and grounded color naming remain poorly calibrated. The strongest
split appears in Task C: tested open-weight endpoints show
daylight-band central-tendency anchors, while frontier endpoints
reduce CCT error — partly through ColorChecker-template priors,
as the non-CC control reveals. The benchmark is limited to synthetic chart stimuli, a single
prompt per task, and sRGB-based rather than spectral rendering;
we plan to address these in the next benchmark version.
